en: Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the *Aparokṣānubhava* with its commentary.
Oṃ! To Śrī Hari, the Supreme Bliss, the Teacher, the Lord—
I bow to that which is all-pervading and the cause of all worlds.
Direct experience (*aparokṣānubhūti*) is declared by the wise to be for the attainment of liberation; it should be observed again and again with diligent effort.
Through the performance of the duties of one's own caste and stage of life, and through austerity that pleases Lord Hara, the fourfold means beginning with detachment shall arise for men.
Detachment toward sense objects extends from Brahmā down to the level of stationary beings.
Just as there is detachment from the excrement of a crow, that indeed is stainless. 4.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Now begins the vernacular commentary on the work *Aparokṣānubhava*. Verse 1.
Śaṅkarasvāmī has said that whatever experience is beyond words, I shall express it in the vernacular so that everyone may understand it. This work is in *caupāī* meter;
Śrī Hari is its form, which is supreme bliss.
The teacher is the Lord Īśvara;
he is all-pervasive and the cause of all worlds—
to him I offer my salutations a thousand times.
The goal is realized for one who has attained liberation; I declare that very thing to be direct knowledge (jñāna-pratyakṣa).
Therefore, O practitioners, exert yourselves with effort.
Constantly keeping this reflection in one's heart, one should observe the duties of one's own stage of life (*āśramadharma*);
by performing that austerity, Lord Hari becomes pleased. There are four means of accomplishment for a person.

Having carefully considered detachment and the rest, these four means are said to be: detachment, discrimination, tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth. First, the nature of detachment for one seeking liberation is described: whatever enjoyments exist on earth, from Brahma downwards— [Verse 3] (The first half of the verse continues as above) ... [the second half follows: ... all those are like a dream; therefore, O mind, abandon them. Do not be attached even to the pleasures of heaven, for they too are subject to destruction. That which is known to be as pure as a crow's droppings is called stainless detachment; it carries away the impurities of passion and the like. 4.

The eternal nature of the Self is indeed the Seer, while that which is its opposite is the seen; such a firm conviction is the true discrimination of reality. The constant abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanā) is what is designated by the term "tranquility" (śama).

The practice of remaining outside the sphere of what is to be suppressed is called *adama*. Turning away from sense objects is indeed the supreme cessation; the endurance of all sufferings is considered auspicious *titikṣā*.
Devotion to the words of the teachers of the Vedas is renowned as faith (śraddhā),
while one-pointedness of mind toward the true object is remembered as concentration (samādhi).
O Creator, how might my liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra ever come to pass?
Thus, this extremely firm intellect is to be called the state of seeking liberation (mumukṣutā).
Now, the nature of discernment (viveka) is being described.
(Verse 9)
When one realizes that the self is eternal and knows that all visible things are subject to destruction,
only then does such certainty arise.
Know that fear is itself solitude; now, the sixfold wealth consisting of tranquility (*śama*), self-control (*dama*), and so forth, is being described.
That which consists in the constant abandonment of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) is what is called the very nature of tranquility (*śama*).
The sage utters that this nature of self-restraint (*dama*) consists in the subduing of the outward functions of the senses;
this is called renunciation (*uparati*), wherein the mind remains withdrawn from sense objects.
That which is called supreme cessation is itself the observer of all sufferings;
that which is of the nature of happiness is forbearance (titikṣā). Faith in the Vedas and the words of the Guru regarding the objects of the senses [is required]. 7.
They said with clear faith:
"We shall keep watch over the funeral pyre;
whatever you say will be done. O Hari, this world is a bondage, they said.
The firm conviction that "when and how shall I be liberated?"—
that which has become such is called *mumukṣutā*.
O noble one! A person who desires his own welfare and seeks the attainment of knowledge must indeed perform this investigation, endowed with the means already described.
Supreme knowledge does not arise through investigation or other means, just as no object appears without light. Who am I? How was this born? And who indeed exists as the knower? || 11 ||
"What is the grasping (upādāna) here? Such is this inquiry:
'I am not the aggregate of elements that is the body, nor likewise am I the aggregate of senses.
This is a certain inquiry distinct from that, and such is the truth. (12-13)

When the manifold volitions, which are the cause of the world of ignorance, have been dissolved by the knowledge of the Omniscient One, such an investigation as this is for one who has attained liberation through the practice of the means. 14.
O practitioner of the means! [This is said] to the one who is liberated.

One should perform inquiry into that person who is joined with the three bodies (*trikāya*); from this, knowledge arises for the sake of attaining perfection. Without the dissolution of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), knowledge does not arise.

What proof can be given that it exists? For just as without the light of the sun and other sources, a jar or similar object is neither present nor perceived. Who am I? What has been born? How much? 11. I am he; who has arisen? How many?
Who taught that the world has a creator?
And who has considered the name of what the cause of the world might be? [If one does so], the material body will cease to exist. 12.

Hoṃ han bhinsag lam ūha na hitāte inako sākṣī maiṃ hauṃ, janī yāko nāma bicāre tanī. 13. Yaha sadya jaga ajñānate bhaya. "Oṃ! Han, bhinsag, lam, ūha—there is no witness for these other than Me; know that I am their witness. 13. This entire world has arisen immediately from ignorance."
Knowledge is the mother of fear;
it is a great abyss that creates manifold conceptualizations.
One should reflect upon its name as "discrimination."
14–15. Furthermore, that which is the single, subtle, and imperishable material cause (*upādāna*) of these two is just like the analysis of clay, jars, and so forth; such is this investigation.
"I alone am subtle, the knower, the witness, the truly imperishable; I am that—of this there is no doubt. Such is this inquiry.
Those who perceive the unity of these two—what ignorance could be greater than that? (16)
The Self is partless, singular, and one, yet it is enveloped by many bodies;
the Self is the controller within, while the body is the controlled exterior. Those who perceive such oneness between the two—what ignorance could be greater than that? (17–18)
Wisdom consists of ignorance of the Self, while the body is composed of flesh and is impure;
those who perceive an identity between these two—what ignorance could be greater than that? Only he who perceives the one Cause of the universe [is free from such ignorance].

That which is subtle and indestructible is just like the clay that is the cause of pots and other objects; when one reflects upon its name, it is "I," the subtle, singular Knower. Furthermore—15. [It is] the subtle, the one Knower. And...

The witness is the eternal and indestructible; he who hears this is I—of this there is no doubt. Only those who have cultivated their intellect know his name as the "Consideration" (vicāra). 16. The Self is partless and one.
The body is merely a great covering; therefore, those two [the self and the body] appear as one. What ignorance could there be beyond this? (17) Look within at the Self, which is the support.
Having restrained the body externally, he again beholds those two as one; what ignorance could be greater than this? 18. He perceives the Self as pure and consisting of knowledge.
This body is composed of flesh and is utterly impure; he who sees these two as one—
what greater ignorance than that could there be?
The self-luminous and pure [consciousness] is called the body when it is characterized by tamas; to perceive the identity of these two—what ignorance could be greater than that? (19-20)
The self is indeed of the nature of existence and impermanent, while the body is non-existent and permanent;
to perceive the identity of these two—what ignorance could be greater than that? The luminosity of the self is that which illumines all objects.
Just as there is no light from fire and such at night because of the darkness,
so it is with this body; for alas, the deluded person persists in holding the notion "I am the body," even while always perceiving objects like a jar through the sense of "this is mine."
I am indeed Brahman—equal, peaceful, and characterized by existence, consciousness, and bliss; I am not this body, which is of an unreal nature. This is what is called "knowledge" by the wise.
The Self is pure, luminous, and conscious.

The body is inert and composed of darkness (tamas); he alone who perceives these two as one is beyond ignorance—what greater ignorance could there be? (20) The Self is eternal and of the nature of truth.
The body is impermanent, unreal, and illusory; O friend, whoever sees these two as one—what ignorance could there be greater than that? That very light belongs to the Self. 21. Therefore...
All objects appear as if they were moving, yet the light of the sun and other luminaries does not; thus the day becomes such that the night does not exist.
I am that very same Sachchidananda; there is no body, for it is unreal.
That which the wise call "knowledge" is this [realization].
I am changeless, formless, blameless, and immutable.
This body is not I, for it is of an unreal nature; it is called "knowledge" by the wise.
I am ultimately free from disease, free from appearance, and free from conceptual construction;
I am not this body, which is of an unreal nature—thus it is said by the wise that I am "Knowledge.
I am called the one who is without qualities, without action, eternal, and eternally liberated.
I am not this body, which is of an unreal nature; I am called "knowledge" by the wise.
I am stainless, immovable, infinite, pure, undecaying, and immortal.
I am not this body, which is of an unreal nature; I am called "knowledge" by the wise.
Having abandoned that which is considered the ornament of your own body and known as the "Person" (Puruṣa), O sir, why do you make yourself empty and devoid of form, transcending the body?
You are changeless and formless.
He is imperishable, faultless, and the essential reality;
the body is unreal, which the wise describe as mere knowledge. 25
May they be free from disease, free from appearance,
free from conceptual construction, and be all-pervading light;
may there be no body, for that which exists is unreal.
The wise call that knowledge which is devoid of qualities, inactive, and eternal. 26.
May I be eternally liberated and infallible;
may I not be the body, which is unreal.
For those wise ones whose knowledge is unimpaired, I am that very one—pure, immovable, and infinite.
I am pure, undecaying, and immortal; this is certain. Listen, there is no attachment to the body for one who is wise—this is what the men of knowledge declare.
He who considers the self to be the body is a fool; that which transcends the body is the Ancient Person (Purāṇa-Puruṣa) described by the Vedas as the true ornament.

Why do you describe it as empty? (28) The disciple’s words are that one should know You as the Person beyond the body; this is called "knowledge," yet it has become empty. The Guru’s words state that the Self is the subject of the Veda (Brahmī Śruti), described as distinct from the body. (29) "Listen to Your own Self through scripture and reasoning as the Person, who is beyond the body, eternally existent, and beautiful to behold for those like you. (30)
The Supreme, known by the word "I," exists as one alone;
how could that Being, having attained oneness with grossness, become the embodied person? The "I" is established as the seer, while the body exists as the object of sight.
Since the teaching is "I am the same," how could the embodied one be the person?
(32) "I am devoid of modification, whereas the body is always subject to modification"—this is directly perceived; how then could the embodied one be the person? (33)
Since she has determined the characteristics of a man by hearing that [the soul] is "other than" [the body], how could the embodied being be a man? (34) [Cau0]
O fool, listen:
seek the Self, which shines forth when described through scripture and reasoning as transcending the body; for that is the cause by which the world lives.
That very [Self] is extremely invisible; it is known through the weight of the scriptures. Know it by means of the word "I" (ahaṃśabda), which is one and transcends all else.
Behold that which is manifold within the gross body.

How can that person be truly happy? (31) He is the seer of objects and the like, yet he considers this body to be the object of sight; having heard and understood this, behold well how this body of mine is but a mere plaything.
How can the body of a person ever become free from the thirty-two transformations? That which is devoid of the six transformations is the true body;
this very body is always joined with transformations—this is direct, perceptible evidence.
How can that person exist? He is the Puruṣa who transcends all;
the Śruti describes His characteristics, and the wise have described Him as such. 33.
"How will the body of Puruṣa be formed?
[In response: "In the hymn named 'Puruṣasūkta,' it is stated that 'all this is indeed Puruṣa. (34)

It is also said: "How could the person be embodied, since he is declared by the Śruti to be unattached? And in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka as well, how could the person be embodied, being untouched by endless impurities? (35-36)
And in that very context, it is declared: "The Person is indeed self-luminous.
How could this embodied being be something insentient or illuminated by another? For even in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), the Self has been described as distinct from the body.
If he were eternal, he would enjoy that fruit immediately upon the arrival of the body.
But how could this person be eternal, given that the subtle body (liṅga) is joined with many things, is mobile, visible, subject to modification, non-pervasive, and of an unreal nature? || 38-39 ||
He who is the Supreme Person for all,
exactly as described in the Brahma-sūkta— that very one the Śruti declares with certainty as the authoritative source.

How can a man possess a beautiful body? (35) The Śruti declares that there are innumerable men; as it is stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, look at how each one is enveloped by infinite impurities.
How can the body be the Self? (36) In that very *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, the Person is called self-luminous; one should see that which illumines the inert body.
How can the body be the self? (37) That which was stated in the Karma-kāṇḍa is this:
the self is seen as distinct from the body, because it departs after experiencing the fruits of its actions.
Behold the many lingas endowed with bodies; they are born from fear, fickle, perceptible, and subject to transformation.
Know them to be unreal in form, non-pervasive, and insubstantial.
How can that Self be [described]?
39 Thus, the Self is other than the two bodies; it is the Person, the Lord, the Self of all, possessing all forms, transcending all, and I am the imperishable. 40

Thus, by means of the distinction between the self and the body, the unreality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) has been established through the aforementioned science of reasoning; what further human goal (*puruṣārtha*) remains?
Thus, by the distinction between the self and the body, the notion that the body is the self has been refuted.
Now, the unreality of the distinction between bodies is clearly stated:
because consciousness is of a single nature, a division is never logical; the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) should be known as false, like the snake perceived in a rope or a house.
Just as through the ignorance of its nature a rope instantly appears as a serpent,
so too does the pure Consciousness itself manifest directly in the form of the entire universe. (44) Thus,
these two appear distinct from the body.

The Self is the Person, the Swift, the Lord, the Beloved; He is the Soul of all, the form of all, and He alone exists as the All; He is the Imperishable. (40) It is said that the Self is distinct from the body.

The delight in making the unreal appear real through the logic described in the treatises on reasoning—that is what is called human effort (puruṣārtha) in this context. One should perceive the self by distinguishing it from the body. 41.

Therefore, that very Self must be established within the body; now, since the distinction between bodies is unreal, I shall describe it as clearly as I am able. (42) Know that the conscious principle is of a single form.
I do not speak of the logic of duality; know the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) to be false, just as one perceives a snake where there is only a rope.
Just as a snake sheds its slough, so too is consciousness; it manifests directly in the form of the universe. 44
No phenomenal expansion (prapañca) exists apart from Brahman;
therefore, this entire phenomenal world is Brahman alone and nothing else.
The relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is false, according to the teaching that "the Self is everything."
When the supreme reality is thus known, how can there be any occasion for misfortune?
Indeed, multiplicity has been refuted by the Śruti through its own mouth;
how could another appearance exist while the non-dual cause remains established? (46–47)
Even the faults are ordained by the Śruti; O Death, he goes from death to death.
A man who sees multiplicity here is deceived by Māyā.
All beings are born from Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Therefore, one should ascertain that these [elements] are indeed Brahman alone;
for know that Brahman is the cause of the world—
do not consider anyone else to be the thief.
O Father, know that this entire phenomenal world is Brahman alone and nothing else; understand that both the pervaded and the pervader are false,
for all is the Self— thus should you hold these words as true.
When the supreme reality is known in this way,
where then can one speak of dualistic perception? (46) Having ascertained it by looking into my own mouth,
I find that the Vedas do not dwell upon any other reality.
How can duality appear when non-dual Brahman has become manifest? O wise one, know that the vision of difference is ordained by the Śruti;
it is through this that birth and death occur. 47.
Only that man who perceives this diversity as an illusion is truly deluded;
he alone who sees it is the Supreme Soul and Brahman. 48.
He who is the father of all beings is the father of this one as well; know him to be Brahman, and believe that there is nothing else apart from Brahman. 49
"The Veda proclaimed that Brahman alone bears all names, various forms, and all actions in their entirety.
And for that which is born from gold, its nature as gold is eternal. (50)
Likewise, the status of being Brahman belongs to Brahman as he is being born.
That deluded soul who remains making even the slightest distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman)— fear has been declared for him.
Where duality arises from ignorance, there one perceives another; but when one regards everything as the Self, there is no other perceived at all.
For one who realizes that all beings are indeed the Self, [there is no distinction].
For him there would be no delusion, nor grief arising from a second;
for whatever diverse names and forms are seen, nothing exists apart from Brahman.
Know all karma to be Brahman alone;
this is the certainty declared by the Śruti as authoritative proof. (50) Just as that which is produced from gold is certainly gold itself.
O Brahman, know that which is born from Brahman;

do not entertain even the slightest doubt regarding this. (51) There is but a slight difference between the individual soul (jīvātman) and the Supreme Soul (paramātman). Those who perceive [a greater] difference...
Know that such a person is a deluded soul;
recognize the fear of birth and death. From ignorance, duality arises, and it is that very ignorance which perceives it there. 52.
Know that when the Self is realized, nothing else remains; there, one must have firm conviction. (53) When all beings are known as the Self, every delusion of duality vanishes.
Seeing that there is no sorrow, delusion, or fear therein, one realizes that very Self as the non-dual;

this Self indeed exists as Brahman itself by virtue of being the self of all. .1sn.1so.1sp.1sq.1sr.1ss.1st.1su.1sv.1sw.1sx.1sy.1sz.1ta.1tb.1tc.1td.1te.1tf.1tg.1th.1ti.1tj.1tk.1tl.1tm.1tn.1to.1tp.1tq.1tr.1ts.1tt.1tu.1tv.1tw.1tx.1ty.1tz.1ua.1ub.1uc.1ud.1ue.1uf.1ug.1uh.1ui.1uj.1uk.1ul.1um.1un.1uo.1up.1uq.1ur.1us.1ut.1uu.1uv.1uw.1ux.1uy.1uz.1va.1vb.1vc.1vd.1ve.1vf.1vg.1vh.1vi.1vj.1vk.1vl.1vm.1vn.1vo.1vp.1vq.1vr.1vs.1vt.1vu.1vv.1vw.1vx.1vy.1vz.1wa.1wb.1wc.1wd.1we.1wf.1wg.1wh.1wi.1wj.1wk.1wl.1wm.1wn.1wo.1wp.1wq.1wr.1ws.1wt.1wu.1wv.1ww.1wx.1wy.1wz.1xa.1xb.1xc.1xd.1xe.1xf.1xg.1xh.1xi.1xj.1xk.1xl.1xm.1xn.1xo.1xp.1xq.1xr.1xs.1xt.1xu.1xv.1xw.1xx.1xy.1xz.1ya.1yb.1yc.1yd.1
Having heard this definitive teaching established in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka,
[he realized that] even though this world is experienced and capable of practical transaction, it is unreal, like a dream sublated by a subsequent moment. || 55-56 ||

The world exists in both dream and waking; yet in dream there is no waking, nor in waking is there dream. For both, dissolution does not exist. These three alone are false, being fashioned from the three qualities (guṇas).
The seer of this [world] is beyond the qualities (guṇa), eternal, and indeed of the nature of pure consciousness.
Just as the delusion of a jar in clay, or the persistence of silver in mother-of-pearl,
so too the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) within Brahman is not seen by one who perceives correctly.
This individual soul is Brahman; one who knows it as the Self of all has made this determination according to the true revelation (śruti).
In this world of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, whatever worldly transactions are seen,
they are given as mere experience; they are of an unreal nature, just like a dream.
All that belongs to the waking state has perished; it is as if asleep. (56) A dream does not exist within the waking state, nor does any waking state exist within a dream;
neither is found within deep sleep.
Therefore, deep sleep (suṣupta) is not to be found among them; 57. hence, know all three to be false and consider them as fashioned by the three qualities (guṇas). Seek that One who is their witness.

That consciousness alone is eternal and beyond all qualities (58). Just as the perception of a pot in clay is a delusion, and the error of silver in mother-of-pearl is likewise, so too is the notion of a "jīva" within Brahman a delusion.
No distinct deliberation regarding these is perceived.
(59) Just as there are names such as "pot" for clay, "earring" for gold, and the designation "silver" for mother-of-pearl, so too is the term "jīva" applied to others. (60)
Just as there is blueness in the sky, as there is water in a desert, and as there is personhood in a post, so too is the universe in the conscious Self (cidātman).
Just as a ghost exists in an empty space, and as is the city of the Gandharvas;
Just as there is the appearance of two moons in the sky, so does the world exist within the Truth (satya).

Just as water alone manifests abundantly through waves and billows, and as copper indeed appears in the form of vessels, so too does the nature of the Self (ātmatā) appear within the multitude of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍa).

Just as clay is called by the name "pot" and threads are called by the name "cloth," so too does consciousness shine as the world; that which is to be known is nothing other than its own absence [of inherent existence]. (64) Just as clay is said to be the name of the pot...

Just as one who possesses many gold earrings and fine pearls and silver bracelets knows them to be such, so too is the individual soul (jīva) said to exist within Brahman; it is like the blueness perceived within the sky. 60. Just as there is blueness within the sky...

Just as one might perceive a ghost in a deserted house, so do people perceive the world within Brahman. (61) Just as one might mistake a pillar for a man, or the earth for water, so too is the world perceived within Brahman. (61) Just as one might perceive a ghost in a deserted house...
Just as the city of Gaṃdharva is seen in the sky, so is the world described within Brahman; just as all waves are seen as nothing but water. 62.
If a reflection appears for even a moment, know that the vessel itself is the mirror; likewise, consider the world to be Brahman alone. (63) Just as a pot is called "earth" by name...
Just as the name "cloth" refers to the threads [that compose it], so too the name "world" is Brahman alone; he who knows that absence [of duality] knows Him. 64
Indeed, all worldly transactions are performed by people through Brahman;
out of ignorance, they do not recognize it, just as one does not recognize clay in a jar or water in a snake.
The relationship of cause and effect exists eternally, just as it does between a jar and its clay.
In the same way, when the world-appearance (prapañca) is grasped here through scripture and reasoning as being non-different from Brahman—
just as a jar is grasped as nothing but clay by the power of its material cause— so too,
within this world-appearance which is about to be described, it is Brahman alone that shines forth as the luminous reality.

The Self is indeed eternally pure, yet it always appears as impure, just as a rope of two strands is constantly perceived by the ignorant; and just as a pot is made of clay, so too is the body composed of consciousness.
This distinction between self and non-self is falsely constructed by the wise; all people are seen engaging in worldly activities, while no one else is performing [such] Brahmanic acts.

Out of ignorance, one does not recognize that which is present in all jars and other objects as the "dead" [unmanifest] cause; just as the clay is eternally the cause within the effect, the jar, it is truly so.
Thus, having examined both scripture and reasoning,
one sees that this entire phenomenal world is nothing but Brahman. Just as when a jar is perceived, it is the very same clay that is perceived.
Just as when the world is perceived, it is Brahman itself that is being perceived; likewise, though the Self is eternally pure, that which appears otherwise as impure is indeed that very same Self.
Just as the wise and the ignorant appear as two distinct types, so too, just as one perceives a jar made of clay,
one should likewise perceive that very same thing as consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmaya*).
The ignorant person who creates this false distinction between self and non-self is like [perceiving] a rope as a snake or mother-of-pearl as silver. (69)
Just as the earth is determined by one who is deluded to be a pot,
and threads are determined to be a cloth, so too is the Self determined to be the body by one who is deluded. (70–71)
The deluded person determines gold to be a golden earring, mercury to be water, and likewise determines the Self to be the body;
they determine a post to be a man, and a mirage to be water.
Just as wood is determined to be a house and iron to be a sword by one who is not deluded, so too the body and the self are determined [as distinct] by one who is not deluded. (73–74)
Just as one perceives a rope as a snake, or believes silver to exist in a seashell,
such indeed are those deluded men.
Who says that the body is the self? (70) Just as the earth is known by the name "pot" and the same threads are considered a "cloth," so too do the ignorant perceive that very [self] in such ways.
Who says the body is the self? (Verse 71) Just as one might mistake gold for an earring or water for a wave,
such are the deluded men.
Who says that the body is the self? Just as one who perceives a pillar as a person knows it for what it is, or as one speaks of a mirage as water—such are those deluded men. 72.
Who says that the body is the self? Those who perceive it as such are like one who, having fashioned a block of wood into the shape of a sword, considers it to be iron;
such people are indeed fools.

Who says that the body is the self? (74) Just as a tree or its reflection may sometimes appear in water, so too does one perceive the state of being the body within the self due to the influence of ignorance. (75)
Just as everything appears flickering to a man traveling in a boat, so too does one perceive the state of having a body in the Self due to the influence of ignorance.
Indeed, just as yellowness appears to someone in a white object because of a defect [in the eye].
In the same way, through the power of ignorance, one perceives the self as having a body;
just as everything appears illusory to eyes prone to wandering, so too does one perceive the self as having a body through the power of ignorance.
Just as a whirling firebrand appears as a circle like the sun due to its rapid rotation,
so too does one perceive the self as having the nature of a body through the power of ignorance. Just as one sees the reflection of a tree in water—
The light of the three Vedas is itself the Self within the body; through ignorance, people perceive it as such. (76) This occurs for those in whom there is a defect of the eyes.
One perceives yellow in what is white; likewise, through ignorance, one sees the body within the self (ātman), just as the eyes are deluded by that which is [actually] moving. 77.

Everything appears as delusion; likewise, within the body, one perceives the self through ignorance alone. Just as a person wandering in confusion might swallow something [unreal], so too does one perceive. 78. Just as a person wandering in delusion might swallow [a mirage].
Just as one sees the orb of the sun, so too does one see the body within the self; it is through ignorance that one perceives them as such. 79
Just as the vastness of all things appears as something extremely remote when viewed through a magnifying glass, so too does one perceive the body within the Self due to the power of ignorance.
Likewise, the grossness of all entities appears [as subtle] through a lens.
In the same way, through the power of ignorance, one perceives the self as having the nature of a body;
just as one perceives water in a glass vessel or a glass vessel in water, so too, through the power of ignorance, one perceives the self as having the nature of a body.
Just as a person perceives the nature of fire in a gem, or the nature of a gem in fire, so too does one perceive the nature of a body in the Self due to the influence of ignorance;
just as someone might experience a confusion of directions out of delusion.
In the same way, through the power of ignorance, one perceives the self as being the body;
that which is far away appears as if it were rolling nearby.
In that same way, through ignorance, they perceive the body within the Self; just as all small objects appear large when viewed through a magnifying glass. 80.
In the same way, through ignorance, they perceive the body within the self; just as one perceives earth and water in glass,
and then perceives the glass within the water.
In the same way, through ignorance, they perceive the body within the self; just as one might mistake a jewel for fire,
thinking the jewel to be of the nature of fire.
In the same way, through ignorance, they perceive the body within the self; just as one suffers from a confusion of directions who calls the east the west. 83.
In that same way, through ignorance, they perceive the body within the Self; that very [Self] shines forth as the moon running amidst the true nectar of the clouds. 84.
In the same way, through the power of ignorance, one perceives the Self as having a body;
just as the moon appears to someone [in water] with a flickering nature, so too, through the power of ignorance, one perceives the Self as having a body. || 85-86 ||

Thus, through the fault of [identifying with] the self, the superimposition of the body arises; that very [superimposition] is dissolved in the Supreme Self through the thorough knowledge of the Self.
[One attains] the knowledge of the entire world, including the moving and the stationary, as being the Self.
Since all things are non-existent, how can there be a body or a self?
O King of great splendor, having constantly realized the Self and experiencing all that has been set in motion by past karma, you ought not to feel distress. 88–89.
Just as a cloud moving in the sky does not diminish the majesty of the moving moon, so too is the relationship between the body and the self.
Out of ignorance, they see it as such; having perceived the moon reflected in the water,
they say that it moves as the water moves.

In this same way, through ignorance, they perceive the body within the Self; that very ignorance which perceives the Self as being of the form of the body. 86. It is that very ignorance which knows the Self as having the nature of the body.
When that very self became knowledge and merged into the Supreme Self, it realized that all this world—whether stationary or moving—is nothing but the Self. 87.
Whatever exists, it was known by the Self alone.
When fear arises from the non-existence of all things,
it is then that one speaks of the distinction between the body and the self. Therefore, O wise one, recognize the Self and spend your time in that very state.
All *prārabdha* karma is exhausted through experience;
do not worry about it, whether it be pleasure or pain.
(89) Once the knowledge of the Self (*adhyātmavijñāna*) has arisen, *prārabdha* no longer exists.
The second [view] is heard in the scriptures; that is now being refuted.

Once the dawn of the knowledge of reality has occurred, no longer does *prārabdha* (the momentum of past karma) exist, just as for one who has awakened, the body and so forth have ceased to be, like a dream—understand this. 90–91.
That which is known as *prārabdha*— the karma from previous births—
is never at all present for a person, because there is no other birth for him.
Just as a body is superposed in a dream, so indeed is this very body.
How can there be birth for that which is superimposed? In the absence of birth, how can there be persistence?
Ignorance is taught by the Vedāntins to be the material cause of the phenomenal world, just as clay is for a pot; if that ignorance is destroyed, where would the universe be? (93–94)
Even when self-knowledge has arisen, that which is ordained by past action (prārabdha) does not escape;
this is what has been heard within the scriptures.
He who casts away much that is distant does not exist; even after knowledge has arisen, whatever remains of *prārabdha* persists,
for the body and such are like a dream.
How can there be a prārabdha when [the Self] exists? That which is called prārabdha is merely the karma from previous births;
upon the dawn of knowledge, even that birth is said to be destroyed.

Where can they remain once *prārabdha* has begun? (92) Just as objects appear to the body in a dream, so too do they appear to the body in the waking state; thus, the birth of that [dream-body] is not possible.

The *prārabdha* karma of this birth is said to have been exhausted (93). Ignorance and consciousness are both the causes of the world, just as clay is the cause of pots; the scripture says that as soon as that ignorance is removed, [the world ceases].

The universe is not seen anywhere; even then, (94) just as one who, out of delusion, abandons the rope and grasps at a snake, so too does the person of dull intellect perceive the world without realizing its true nature. (95)
When the nature of the rope is fully understood, the notion of a "piece of snake" ceases; likewise, when the substratum is known, the phenomenal world (prapañca) becomes emptiness.
Since the body itself is part of this phenomenal world, how can there be any persistence of prārabdha-karma?
The Śruti declares that *prārabdha* karma exists for the sake of awakening ignorant people;
"his karmas are exhausted when He, the higher and the lower, is seen.
The multiplicity [of karmas] was clearly sung in the Śruti for the purpose of negating that [very existence]. 97–98.
It is said by the wise that this [assertion] is forcibly made because it leads to two undesirable consequences:
the abandonment of the Vedānta doctrine and the negation of knowledge; for such is the Śruti: "Whereby one knows.
Just as one who abandons the rope...
The serpent says: "He who wanders about in that very manner, having abandoned Brahman, sees the world with a deluded intellect. (95) When knowledge of the rope arose for him, [he saw it as such].

When one is free from the fear of snakes, then one knows that very thing to be Brahman; when the world is no longer perceived anywhere, then it is known as unreal. 96. When [the world] is perceived, it is known as unreal.
When one encounters *prārabdha*, the ignorant do not attain awakening; therefore, the Śruti, for the purpose of explaining the nature of the Self, has described *prārabdha*.
(97) For the sake of the vision of the Self, the Śruti has indeed spoken thus.
The description of *prārabdha* has been completed [verse 97]. If all karma is destroyed through the vision of the Self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), then what would become of *prārabdha* at that time?
The Śruti openly declares this very statement: "That which the ignorant call ignorance is indeed the inexhaustible Prārabdha.
Thus, when both faults are incurred, [the wise remain unshaken].
I shall now describe those two faults; first, observe the fault regarding liberation, and then hear that very second fault.
If the lineage of the tradition of knowledge is severed, this is indeed another fault; furthermore, it results in the ruin of the Vedānta doctrine.
Know this for certain:
that very thing which arises as knowledge when determined is what the Vedas declare; do not harbor doubt in your heart. 99
Next, I shall describe the fifteen limbs for the attainment of what was previously mentioned;
by means of all these, one must constantly practice *nididhyāsana* (contemplation).
Without constant practice, the realization of the *saccidātman* (the Being-Consciousness-Bliss Self) does not occur.

Therefore, one who desires to know Brahman and seeks its ultimate good should meditate upon it for a long time. Restraint (yama), observance (niyama), renunciation (tyāga), silence (mauna), [proper] place and time, posture (āsana), the root-lock (mūlabandha), equilibrium of the body, and the steadiness of the gaze—[these are the means]. || 101-102 ||
The restraint of the vital breath (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā),

meditation on the Self (dhyāna), and absorption (samādhi) are declared to be the limbs [of yoga] in their proper sequence. The restraint of the aggregate of the senses arises from the realization that "all is Brahman."
That which is proclaimed as "Yama-yama" should be practiced again and again.
Now I shall tell you that which is beneficial for one who has attained knowledge, regarding the five limbs of yoga.
Perform all these yogic practices; O wise one, always consider this nididhyāsana as essential. Without daily practice for a hundred days, the attainment of the Self will not occur.

O Father, for one who desires to know and practices the profound meditation on Brahman, this is better than all else: first, the observance of *yama* and *niyama*, then renunciation, followed by silence, and finally, discernment regarding place and time. 101.

Having performed the root-lock (mūlabandha) on the seat, one should then steady the body and fix the gaze; then one performs breath control (prāṇāyāma), followed by withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) and concentration (dhāraṇā). 102.
The Self is perceived through meditation and concentration; all these limbs have been described in sequence. (103) Now, the restraints (yamas) will be explained.
He who realizes that Brahman alone pervades all worlds and thereby subdues all his senses—
he is called the most excellent Yama.
By practicing that very same thing again and again—[as it is said:
"A continuous flow of the homogeneous and the rejection of the heterogeneous is indeed the rule [leading to] supreme bliss; therefore, this is practiced by the wise through discipline. (104–105)
Renunciation [comes] from perceiving the world of manifold forms as being of the nature of consciousness;
for this renunciation is honored by the great, since it consists of immediate liberation. From which words turn back, along with the mind, having failed to reach it—
That which is the silence to be reached by yogis, that alone should always be known by the wise.
Since words turn back from it, who is able to speak of it? Even if the phenomenal world were to be described, it too would be devoid of sound.

Thus, that which is known as the natural silence of the virtuous is true *mauna*; however, the silence of speech is what is prescribed for the ignorant by those who discourse on Brahman. (109) Now, the observances (*niyamas*) are described.
One who practices the mental state of the form of Brahman,
having abandoned the mental state of the form of the world—
that alone is called "niyama" (observance); this is what its name is said to be.
O Niyama, O Supreme Bliss, the wise man attains this [state]. (105) Now, renunciation is being described:
for one who perceives the One Self, the abandonment of all names and forms occurs.
By performing great renunciation, one is honored;
therefore, O noble one, liberation occurs immediately. 106. Now, "mauna" (silence) is being described: that which cannot be expressed by means of speech.
No one can grasp that [state] through mental effort;
therefore, the wise yogi knows it through silence and always considers his own true form to be that. (107) This is what is called "speech."
That cessation which is beyond speech cannot be described by anyone; to speak of it would be a mere conceptual elaboration.
Even though he is devoid of sound, the thought "one hundred and eight" is uttered for him; this is called silence (*mauna*).
Among the holy men (*sat-puruṣa*), it is revealed that speech is silence, whereas silence is known as ignorance.
The wise man has well explained this:
that place where no person exists in the beginning, the end, or the middle, and which is eternally pervaded by Him—that place is solitary, immortal, and eternal. (109–110)
Because it measures all beings, beginning with Brahmā, by means of its twinkling,
that which is indeed indivisible, non-dual bliss is designated by the word "Time" (Kāla). In that [state], the constant contemplation of Brahman occurs effortlessly.
One should know that to be the true seat, and not any other, which is a seat of ease.
That which is established as the beginning of all beings, the immutable foundation of the universe, wherein the perfected one has entered— that indeed is Siddhāsana.
That which is the root of all beings is the binding of the mind;
this root-binding (mūlabandha) should always be practiced, for it is suitable for royal yogins.
Now, the locations are being described.
Neither at the beginning, nor at the end, nor within the middle is there a world-lord other than the Self;
that which eternally pervades this [Self] is He.
That which is called the seed-place (bījasthāna) is indeed what is called the eternal time;
it is all beings, beginning with Brahmā.

Know that the movement of the breath, its stability, and its dissolution constitute the word "Time" (kāla); that is the true state of unbroken bliss (akhaṇḍānanda). This is called the Sukhāsana. 111. This is called the Sukhāsana.
In the meditation on Brahman, which is blissful and stable in form, there is no sense of duty nor any anxiety;
know that this itself is the true seat.
There is neither going nor a comfortable seat (112); this very state is called the Siddhāsana, because by it all beings become perfected,
and it is that very imperishable substratum of the world.
Among those, one becomes perfected by that which is called *siddhāsana*. (113) Now, the *mūlabandhana* is described;
it is the root of all beings.
The funeral pyre has bondage as its root;
that very root is bondage, which always remains for the yogi who serves the kingdom [of the Self]. (114) One should know equality among all limbs; one merges into Brahman when it is equalized.
Neither should there be equanimity nor straightness like that of a withered tree.
Having made one's vision consist of knowledge, one should behold the world as composed of Brahman; such a vision is supremely noble, not the mere gazing at the tip of the nose.
One should fix the gaze precisely where the cessation of the seer, the act of seeing, and the seen occurs; it is not by looking at the tip of the nose.
This is because all entities, beginning with the mind, are to be meditated upon as being none other than Brahman.
The cessation of all mental fluctuations is called prāṇāyāma. The restraint of the phenomenal world is known as the exhaling breath (recaka);
the mental state "I am indeed Brahman" is declared to be the internal air (pūraka). 118–119.
Now, the equality of the body will be explained: know that all [bodies] are equal like fire;
therefore, taking the Self as equal, for that reason [the body is said to be equal].
115. Knowing this equality, one becomes like a withered tree; no force can prevail against such a person. Now, the method for fixing the gaze will be described:
he who makes his gaze consist of pure knowledge is a true yogi.
When one perceives the world as the form of Brahman, that vision is truly noble;
it is not the mere gazing at the tip of the nose. That which is the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen—[all these are Brahman]. 116.
If all three folds [of the abdomen] are perceived, that very sight is the practice; one should neither look at nor fix the gaze upon the tip of the nose. 117. Now, prāṇāyāma is being described.
When one recognizes all meditations, beginning with the mind, as being of the nature of Brahman,
then all mental fluctuations are restrained; this is why [it is called Samprajñāta Yoga].
Prāṇāyāma is well described as follows: 118. This entire phenomenal world is false; that which is called *recaka* (exhalation) is when one perceives, "I am Brahman."
That which is called *pūraka* is thus described (verse 119). Thereafter, the steadiness of virtuous conduct is *kumbhaka*, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
This [practice] is for the enlightened; for the ignorant, it is merely the affliction of the vital breath. (Verse 120)

Having perceived the self-nature within the objects of the senses, the immersion of the mind [into them] is to be known as *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal); it should be practiced by those seeking liberation,
because wherever the mind goes, there one perceives Brahman.
The commonality of the mind and the state of being the supreme delight of concentration (dhāraṇā) is the abiding in a state of supportlessness through the true practice of "I am indeed Brahman.
This is renowned by the term meditation (dhyāna), bestowing supreme bliss. || 122-123 ||

Through the modification of being changeless and, furthermore, through the modification of having the form of Brahman, the complete forgetting of [other] modifications is rightly termed the knowledge of samādhi.
That true modification becomes perfectly steady.
That which is called *kumbhaka* is indeed *prāṇāyāma* for the wise; this [practice] of pressing the nostrils is said by the ignorant to be [merely that]. 120. Now, *pratyāhāra* is described.
Recognizing sound and the other objects as the Self, and establishing the mind in consciousness, one should perceive the well-known practice of pratyāhāra (withdrawal).
The seeker of liberation should practice yoga (verse 121). Now, the concentrations (dhāraṇās) will be described:
wherever the mind goes, there the yogi [should fix it].
Who sees Brahman there? That very one; therefore, the mind's holding [of that] occurs, which is called by the name *dhāraṇā*. (122) Now, *ātma-dhyāna* (meditation on the Self) is described.
Know that very thing which is the supportless and unstable state of the true seeker of Brahman to be what is called meditation (dhyāna).
Recognize the giver of supreme bliss (123). Now, samādhi is described:
that which is changeless and free from dualistic movement, which becomes the very form of Brahman.

When all mental fluctuations are forgotten and only pure consciousness remains, that is truly called *samādhi*. Having realized this uncreated bliss, one should practice it with a virtuous person. 924. *Imaṃ cākṛtrimānandaṃ jñātvā sādhūn samabhyaset*.
Once brought under control, he may arise again from the very moment of his dissolution;
thereafter, liberated from all means of practice, he becomes a perfected one, a king among yogis.
His true nature is not an object of the mind, nor is it within the scope of words.
When one is engaged in meditative concentration (samādhi), obstacles arise through the force of destiny:

lack of sustained attention, laziness, longing for sensory enjoyment, lethargy (laya), darkness (tamas), distraction (vikṣepa), relishing the aesthetic flavor (rasāsvāda), and emptiness (śūnyatā). 127.
Thus, one who knows Brahman should gradually abandon this multitude of obstacles.
Through the state of existence, one attains existence; through the state of emptiness, emptiness;
and through the state of Brahman, fullness. Therefore, one should practice that fullness.
Knowing this bliss to be uncreated, the saint practices it as long as this [mind] remains under the control of the person.
When the mind is attached to China Mahā, then all other spiritual practices are abandoned;
that very one who becomes a perfected king of yogis—
his true nature is not this physical body.
If one speaks by means of mind and speech, then it is called verbal samādhi; but if it occurs through the power of action, then that is indeed the absence of discursive thought (anusaṃdhāna).
O seeker, laziness, longing for enjoyments, absorption in darkness, distraction, and even the tasting of the flavor of life— all these are but emptiness.
One who knows Brahman abandons such obstacles as they increase by employing skillful means. (128) There is an absence of contemplation upon the words of Ṭaṭakā, and there is grief.

Laziness, making effort for worldly enjoyment, absorption in longing for sense objects, sleep, lack of discrimination between what should and should not be done, distraction, relishing memories of sense objects, and mental states such as "I am blessed"—these forms of bliss are defects of the mind. One who possesses the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of attachment, aversion, and so forth is a person of existence (*bhāva-yukta*); one whose mental states are empty of such things is a person of emptiness (*śūnya-yukta*).
The state of Brahman is the complete Brahman; that perfection arises from practice.
Abandoning this worldly activity, one should reach that supreme ground called Brahman. 129.
Those who merely subsist in this way live in vain, for they are equal to beasts; however, those who truly understand their livelihood and, having understood it, cause it to flourish—
they alone are virtuous men, blessed, and kinsmen throughout the three worlds.
Those whose conduct is balanced, increased, and fully matured— they alone have attained the state of Brahmanhood, and not others who merely discourse on Brahman.
Those who are skilled in the discourse on Brahman but lack such conduct are full of passion.
Even they, though diminished by the darkness of ignorance, come again and go away;
they remain for but half a moment without the state consisting of Brahman,
just as Brahmā and the others, Sanaka and the others, and Śuka and the others remain [in that state].
That person who abandons the supremely purifying state of Brahman lives in vain within this world.
Those men are like cattle who do not know the way of Brahman; blessed are those virtuous persons who, having known it, remain ever increasing in that knowledge. (130)
He alone is worthy of worship in the three worlds,
whose disposition remains well-guarded and who has further reached full maturity.
They have not attained even a hundredth part of Brahman; though some one hundred and thirty-two are clever in the discourse on Brahman,
they remain worldly-minded and have not truly entered the state of Brahman.
They are indeed ignorant, for they undergo birth and death again and again; that state which does not last even half a moment, unless it is one whose very nature is absorbed in Brahman. 133.
Know that Brahmā and the others are like grass;
Sanaka and the others, as well as Śuka, are considered equal [to Him]. (134) Through the relationship of cause and effect, they have attained the state of being effects by means of the Cause.
Therefore, through investigation, causality would cease to exist in the absence of an effect.
Now, the pure reality, which is indeed beyond the scope of words, should be perceived again and again by means of the very analogy of the clay and the jar. || 135-136 ||
In this very manner, the mental state (vṛtti) becomes one whose essence is Brahman; thereafter, the knowledge of that state arises for those of pure mind.
First, one should perceive the Person as distinct from the cause.
Furthermore, by means of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), one likewise perceives the effect as eternal.
For one should perceive the cause within the effect, and subsequently abandon the effect; by cutting through the state of causality within one's own self, the sage remains as that which is left over.
That which has the effect as its object is the cause;
there is nothing that has the cause as its object. This is because of the absence of any effect.
If one considers the state of being a cause, then that very pure Brahman which is beyond the reach of mind and speech remains;
it is seen just as clay is seen to be the cause of a pot.

Again and again, through these examples, when the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is examined in this manner, that which consists of Brahman arises; that very [modification] shines forth within the pure mind.
Those [causes] exist as subsequent knowledge (uparāntajñāna). Whatever cause exists prior to the effect,
when the Puruṣa perceives it at the very beginning, he finds that cause within the effect.
Furthermore, when one looks back, that very same thing which was seen as the cause within the effect vanishes;
once the effect is dissolved, its causality also departs from itself. That indeed is it.
That which remains is the sage himself.

(139) Just as a substance is permeated by a powerful force through the nature of its certain determination, so too does a person quickly become that very thing, like the "bee-worm" (bhramara-kīṭa). (140)
For all this, which is invisible and of the nature of existence, is essentially consciousness;
one should constantly contemplate one's own self with vigilance. Having brought the visible to a state of invisibility, one should contemplate it in the form of Brahman.
The wise one should remain in eternal bliss with an intellect filled with the essence of consciousness.
O dear one, when these limbs are combined, it is declared as Rājayoga;
for those whose impurities are somewhat ripened, it is joined with Haṭhayoga.
For those whose minds are fully ripened, it bestows the fivefold perfections alone;
it is easily attained by all who are devoted to their guru and the deity.
Thus ends the *Śrī Aparokṣānubhava*, composed in the vernacular by Jñānadāsa.
By practicing intense contemplation, whatever object is perceived, if certainty arises regarding it,
the person quickly becomes exactly like that.
Just as a bee perceives a worm, whatever form is seen or unseen, this conscious being sees it all; therefore,
one should always remain vigilant within that state.
If one perceives the visible world as invisible and contemplates it solely as the form of Brahman,
then that wise person remains eternally established in bliss. (141)
The intellect attains the state of being filled with consciousness (142). By means of this method, it is called a "royal yoga" (rāja-yoga);
that which is even slightly purified of the nature of the afflictions (kaṣāya) is [so designated].
Yoga, together with its eight limbs, has matured the mind of that one for whom there is true knowledge; he is a devotee of the Guru, who bestows the perfection of absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna).
Success is easily attained by everyone everywhere;
whether at a sacred pilgrimage site or in the house of an outcaste, whoever abandons the body with lost memory attains it.

If, at the end, one attains the fruit of knowledge and reaches the state of liberation (kaivalya) which is free from sorrow, then whether one dies on the road, in urine or excrement, in a house, among outcasts (caṇḍālas), or in a cremation ground— it matters not.
It is said that whether there is effort or not,
upon the end of the body, one attains liberation. (Dohā 2)

The year is Basu-graha-basu (1798), the month of Kārtika, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, on a Friday; know it to be so. At the site of Indraprastha, King Līlākaṭa spoke this knowledge at the door of Rāma;
thus says Jñānadāsa Paramāna. 1-2.
Thus ends the *Aparokṣānubhūti-ṭīkā*, the commentary on the *Aparokṣānubhūti*.
